dims.title: True out-of-sample check with real ETFs

result.dimension: True out-of-sample check with real ETFs (KEY = oos_live): 2026-07-27..2026-11-17, 81 trading days
result.headline: On real ETFs after the freeze (07-27 to 11-17), Friday-close execution: scanner F (TQQQ/TLT/GLD) -10.85%, F3 (IEF) -8.99%, F2 (QLD) -6.03%, Strategy A +6.90%, against NDX -4.01%. That is a bad stretch but not an abnormal one (F3 sits at the 8.4th percentile of 81-day windows, and the 25th percentile among windows with a similar NDX path). Almost all of the loss came from one tail week at full size just before the exit (F3 -13.9%, only 4 worse weeks since 1988). The exit worked: without it F3 would be -22.8%. Real ETFs tracked the model within 0.33pp. Current holdings for F3 and F2: 85% IEF + 15% GLD.

claims.claim: Out-of-sample results on real ETFs reproduce the model exactly, because the spliced sleeves equal the real ETFs in the window. Strategy F as the scanner implements it (TLT) was the worst of the four. Strategy A was the only one with a gain.
claims.evidence: OOS 07-27..11-17, lag 1 (trade at Friday close): (a) F scanner TQQQ/TLT/GLD -10.85%; (b) F3 TQQQ/IEF/GLD -8.99%; (c) F2 QLD vt.30/IEF/GLD -6.03%; (d) A TQQQ/BIL vt.25 +6.90%; July-spec F (proxies) -7.80%. Benchmarks: NDX -4.01%, QQQ -3.89%, QLD -10.84%, TQQQ -18.89% (maxDD -40.1%), 60/40 SPY/IEF -0.87% (SPX-price version -1.07%), 85% IEF/15% GLD -1.92%. Max |real - spliced| in the window is 0. An independent yfinance pull matches the panel to within 2e-7 per day. Weekly drift simulation vs constant-mix differs by 0.1pp or less.

claims.claim: The OOS loss is unpleasant but within normal historical noise for these strategies. It is not evidence that the strategy has broken.
claims.evidence: Percentile of the OOS return among all 81-day windows 1988..2026-07-24 (2010+ only in brackets): a 6.8 (5.8), b 8.4 (6.5), c 9.1 (7.5), d 51.7 (45.4). z-scores: a -1.18, b -1.09, c -1.02. F3's historical 81-day median is +5.1% and its 5th percentile is -11.6%. Among windows where NDX returned within 4pp of -4.0% (about 36 episodes), F3 ranks at the 25.0th percentile and F2 at 25.3. Ranked against a regression on NDX the residual percentiles are 15.6 and 16.7. Percentile of OOS maxDD: F3 14.0, F2 17.3. The same calendar window (Jul 27..Nov 17) ranks 3rd-worst of 39 years for F3, behind only 1988 (-10.6%) and 2011 (-19.6%).

claims.claim: The loss came almost entirely from a single tail week at maximum exposure between the NDX record and the exit. This is a recurring failure mode of the design: full size after a calm, clean trend.
claims.evidence: F3 was +9.86% at the NDX record close of 31,224 on 10-06. From 10-07 to 10-16 it lost -16.38% holding 85% TQQQ (0.06th percentile of 8-day windows). The held week 10-12..10-16 returned -13.88%, the 0.21st percentile; only 4 of 1,944 backtest weeks were worse (1995-07-21, 1996-03-01, 1999-07-23, 2007-03-02). All four had 76-85% TQQQ, vol 10-22% and ER 0.37-0.66 at the decision, the same signature as 10-09-2026 (vol 0.156, ER 0.332). F2's equivalent week was -9.39% (0.36th percentile).

claims.claim: The exposure path explains why F3/F2 trailed Strategy A. The chop and Aug-Sep halvings kept exposure low through the rally, then both lifted in the same week (10-02), moving F3 from 21% to 85% TQQQ just before the drop. A diagnostic rule-removal shows these overlays cost about 13pp in this window. They should not be changed on this evidence, because in-sample they cut maxDD from -49% to -30%.
claims.evidence: Decision log, F3 TQQQ weight: 7/24 37.3%, 7/31 35.9%, August 16.2-21.2%, September 21.2% (seasonal x chop), 10/02 85.0%, 10/09 85.0%. Average TQQQ weight from the freeze to the record was 0.257, while TQQQ itself gained +31.9% over that stretch. Diagnostic F3 OOS: as specified -9.0%; no Aug-Sep -6.4%; no chop -1.4%; neither +4.0%. The corresponding in-sample maxDD/Calmar are -30.0%/0.80, -32.9%/0.73, -46.6%/0.60 and -49.0%/0.58. The record-to-exit loss is -16.4% in every variant.

claims.claim: The EMA-100 exit worked as designed and limited the damage.
claims.evidence: The exit signal came at the Friday 10-16 close (NDX 29,188 < EMA 29,306) and took effect 10-19. Since then F3 and F2 have each returned -0.93%, while QQQ fell -7.45% and TQQQ -24.04%. Counterfactual with the gate removed: F3 OOS -22.8% instead of -9.0% (risk-off phase -16.0% instead of -0.93%, maxDD -32.6%). F2 would have been -15.2% instead of -6.0%.

claims.claim: Treasuries lost money while the strategy was risk-on, as yields rose to about 5.1%: stocks and bonds fell together. TLT, which the scanner uses, made this worse, which confirms the audit's IEF fix. Gold drove the small loss after the exit.
claims.evidence: Risk-on phase P&L as % of starting capital: F3 TQQQ -6.18, IEF -2.37, GLD +0.47, cost -0.06. Scanner F: TQQQ -6.00, TLT -4.00, GLD +0.46. Risk-off phase F3: IEF +0.26, GLD -1.07. TLT costs 1.86pp vs IEF over 81 days (-10.85% vs -8.99%). Diagnostic only: a BIL off-leg would have given -6.5% OOS, but its in-sample Calmar is 0.72 vs 0.80.

claims.claim: The simulated sleeves used for pre-inception history track the real ETFs closely in the current rate regime. The July proxies did not track: in this window alone, gold miners differed from physical gold by 7.3pp.
claims.evidence: OOS real minus sim: TQQQ -0.21pp (TE 2.2%/yr; expected 1-sigma 2.0pp), QLD +0.09pp, QQQ +0.18pp, IEF -0.17pp, TLT +0.05pp, BIL -0.05pp, GLD vs GC=F-0.4% -0.02pp. Strategy level: a -0.26pp, b -0.33pp, c -0.19pp, d -0.23pp. July proxies: GLD -5.22% vs ^XAU miners +2.11% (-7.33pp); TLT vs July synthetic 10y -1.25pp.

claims.claim: Execution timing matters little for live trading since 2010. The OOS advantage of Monday execution is a one-day coincidence. The full-history lag-1 headline is flattered by the 1988-1999 period.
claims.evidence: OOS F3: Friday close -8.99%, Monday close (lag 2) -7.5%, Monday open -5.9%. The difference comes entirely from 10-19, when TQQQ gapped up +4.1% at the open (+3.47pp for Monday-open execution), and 10-05 (-1.69pp for lag 2). In-sample on real ETFs, 2010-02-22..2026-07-24 with drift, F3 CAGR/maxDD/Calmar: Friday close 25.7%/-27.6%/0.93; Monday open 24.8%/-27.2%/0.91; Monday close 26.3%/-29.5%/0.89. For F2: 18.7/0.78, 18.1/0.76, 19.1/0.77. Model F3 CAGR, lag 1 vs lag 2, by era: 1988-99 34.5 vs 27.0; 2000-09 11.4 vs 11.3; 2010-07/2026 25.1 vs 25.8. NDX daily autocorrelation by era: +0.025, -0.069, -0.102. Full in-sample F3: lag 1 24.13%/Calmar 0.80 vs lag 2 22.24%/0.63.

claims.claim: Current holdings as of the last date (2026-11-17): (b) and (c) are fully risk-off. They re-enter only if NDX closes a Friday above roughly 28,890.
claims.evidence: Decided at the 11-13 close and unchanged if the scanner is run at the 11-17 close (NDX 27,002 vs EMA-100 28,968, -6.8%; vol20 0.355; ER 0.260): (b) F3 85% IEF + 15% GLD; (c) F2 85% IEF + 15% GLD; (a) 85% TLT + 15% GLD; (d) 100% BIL. Next decision is the Friday 2026-11-20 close. Risk-on requires NDX(Friday) > EMA(Thursday), about 28,891 (+7.0%) if NDX is flat until then. Re-entry sizes at the current vol: TQQQ 47.9% (b) or QLD 71.8% (c), halved if ER < 0.25.

claims.claim: Weights were decided only from data available at each Friday close, and the simulation is identical to what the live scanner showed.
claims.evidence: Recomputing EMA-100, vol20 and ER20 on NDX data truncated at each of the 17 decision dates and the last date gives a max difference of 0 (1.7e-8 on a 5-year window, as the scanner uses). The scanner state saved on 2026-07-31 is replicated exactly: NDX 28274.2, EMA 28049.0, vol 0.2371, ER 0.15, F = TQQQ 0.359 / TLT 0.491 / GLD 0.15. The yield-curve rule is a no-op on the entire history. Compounding the decision-log weekly returns reproduces each OOS total to 1e-10.

claims.claim: Strategy A's +6.9% is a median outcome for A, not a reason to switch to it. F2's smaller loss than F3 is consistent with the earlier finding that 2x beats 3x on a risk-adjusted basis, but this one window cannot separate them.
claims.evidence: A's OOS return is at the 51.7th percentile of its own 81-day windows. Its worst OOS week was -16.1% and its OOS maxDD -19.1%; in-sample maxDD -67.4%, Calmar 0.45. F2 vs F3 OOS: -6.03% vs -8.99%, maxDD -12.3% vs -17.3%, worst week -9.4% vs -13.9%, but at nearly the same percentiles (9.1 vs 8.4). In-sample Calmar 0.82 vs 0.80.

result.current_read:
On real ETFs since the July freeze (81 trading days, real-ETF returns verified against an independent yfinance pull), the faithful strategies lost money: F3 TQQQ/IEF/GLD -8.99%, F2 QLD/IEF/GLD -6.03%, and the scanner's TQQQ/TLT/GLD version -10.85%. NDX was down 4.01% over the same window. The model's spliced sleeves equal the real ETFs in this window, and the simulated sleeves used before each ETF existed track them within 0.2-0.3pp. The backtest mechanics are therefore faithful, and the OOS numbers are real outcomes, not modelling error.

The loss is in the bad tail of normal: 8-9th percentile of 81-day windows since 1988 (z about -1.1), and 25th percentile among windows with a similar NDX path. The mechanism is specific. The chop and Aug-Sep halvings held F3 at 16-21% TQQQ through the August-September rally, so it was only +9.9% at the NDX record. Both cuts lifted on 10-02, and low vol (15%) set the vol scale to 1.0, so F3 held 85% TQQQ into a -5.5% NDX week. That week cost -13.9%, the 5th-worst F3 week in 38 years. All four worse weeks share the same signature (1995, 1996, 1999, 2007), so this is a recurring, known failure mode, roughly once every 8 years, not a regime break.

The EMA-100 exit then worked: it took effect 10-19, and since then F3/F2 are -0.93% versus QQQ -7.45% and TQQQ -24.0%. Without the gate F3 would be -22.8%. Treasuries lost money during the risk-on phase as the 10y yield rose to about 5.1% (IEF -2.4pp, TLT -4.0pp of capital), the known stocks-and-bonds-down weakness. That makes TLT the worst off-leg and confirms the audit's IEF fix.

Execution timing is second-order in the modern era. Since 2010 on real ETFs, Friday close, Monday open and Monday close give F3 CAGR 25.7%, 24.8% and 26.3% (Calmar 0.89-0.93). The OOS advantage of Monday execution comes entirely from TQQQ's +4.1% opening gap on 10-19. The model's full-history lag-1 advantage comes only from 1988-1999 (F3 34.5% vs 27.0% CAGR; nothing since 2000), so the 1990s part of the headline CAGR should be treated as optimistic.

Current holdings: F3 and F2 hold 85% IEF + 15% GLD, the scanner version 85% TLT + 15% GLD, and Strategy A 100% BIL. The next decision is the Friday 2026-11-20 close. Re-entry needs NDX to close above about 28,890, which is +7.0% from 27,002.

Full results are in update_2026_11/oos_live.json, including the weekly decision log, attribution, percentiles and tracking.
result.recommendation:
1. Change no parameter on the strength of this window. One 81-day draw at the 8-9th percentile is consistent with the backtest. The diagnostic showing the chop and seasonal overlays cost about 13pp here is matched by their in-sample benefit (maxDD -30% vs -49%).
2. Fix the live scanner to IEF instead of TLT, as the audit found. The OOS result confirms it: TLT cost an extra 1.9pp in 81 days, and in-sample maxDD is -40.7% vs -30.0%.
3. Keep the EMA-100 exit exactly as is. It saved about 14pp versus no gate.
4. Choosing between the 2x and 3x versions: F2 (QLD vt .30) had the smaller OOS loss (-6.0% vs -9.0%), drawdown (-12.3% vs -17.3%) and tail week (-9.4% vs -13.9%). This agrees with the earlier finding that 2x beats 3x risk-adjusted across markets, but the preference rests on that prior evidence, not on this window.
5. Current target for both F3 and F2: 85% IEF + 15% GLD. Re-evaluate at the Friday 2026-11-20 close and go risk-on only if NDX closes above about 28,890. At today's vol (35.5%), the re-entry size would be about 48% TQQQ (F3) or 72% QLD (F2), halved if ER < 0.25.
6. Executing Monday at the open or close after a weekend scanner run is acceptable; since 2010 it changes CAGR by under 1pp/yr. The July lag-1 headline should be quoted with the caveat that its advantage over lag 2 comes only from 1988-1999.
7. Set expectations explicitly: about once every 8 years, F3 can lose 14-17% in a single week when it is at full size after a calm trend.
caveats: 81 trading days is a single draw. Percentiles use overlapping windows (about 120 effectively independent 81-day windows since 1988), so the sampling error at the 8th percentile is roughly ±2.5 points.

The historical distribution uses simulated TQQQ before 2010, QLD before 2006 and QQQ before 1999, synthetic bonds before 2002, and monthly-interpolated gold before 2000-09. Percentiles from 2010 onward only (real TQQQ) are 1-2 points lower: F3 6.5, F2 7.5.

The rule-removal and no-gate runs are diagnostics that explain where the OOS P&L came from. They were never used to choose a parameter. Every configuration evaluated is a pre-registered July spec or a benchmark.
The Monday-open variant uses dividend-adjusted yfinance opens with the same 3 bps per turnover. Opening auctions for leveraged ETFs can carry wider spreads than modelled.

Two accounting conventions are reported. The model (common.py) holds constant weights between weekly marks; the drift simulation lets holdings drift between Friday rebalances. They differ by 0.1pp or less OOS.
The 60/40 history uses the ^GSPC price index (no dividends). The SPY total-return version exists only inside the OOS window (-0.87% vs -1.07%) and has no percentile.

The OOS gold sim uses GC=F front-month futures minus 0.40%/yr (the panel's 2000-2004 splice source). Its daily closes are not synchronous with GLD (TE 9.5%/yr), although the cumulative gap is -0.02pp.

The re-entry threshold (about 28,891) assumes NDX stays flat until Thursday 11-19. The exact rule is NDX(Friday close) > EMA-100(Thursday). ER is 0.260, just above the 0.25 chop threshold, so re-entry size could halve.
Strategy A's cash leg is BIL (real). The July research used T-bill rf_d, which is +0.09pp higher over the window.

variants_tested = 110 strategy x mechanics evaluations across 23 configurations: 5 strategies, 6 benchmarks, 2 no-gate counterfactuals and 10 diagnostic rule removals, under the model, real, simulated-sleeve, lag and drift/open mechanics. Execution-timing in-sample checks on the 2010-2026 real-ETF span are included.

verdicts.reason: I re-ran oos_live.py unchanged with its output sent to a scratch file: 0 of the JSON's numeric leaves differ (tolerance 2e-6). A separate engine written from scratch (own EMA/vol/ER, own Friday calendar, own holdings loop, no common.py) gives the same OOS lag-1 results: a -10.847, b -8.995, c -6.032, d +6.902, July-spec -7.799. Lag 2 gives -9.217, -7.493, -5.017, +10.705. My own share-level drift sim gives -10.866, -9.044, -6.068, +6.900. All benchmarks match. The yfinance-vs-panel max daily difference in the window is 1.9e-7, within the claimed 2e-7. However, that check uses the same vendor pulled the same day, so it validates the splice and alignment code, not the prices themselves.

All quoted numbers reproduce: percentiles 6.8/8.4/9.1/51.7, 2010+ figures 5.8/6.5/7.5/45.4, conditional 25.0/25.3 (36 episodes), residual 15.6/16.7, DD percentiles 14.0/17.3, calendar rank 3/39 (1988 -10.6%, 2011 -19.6%). Pre-2000 interpolated gold is not a factor: booking gold at month-end changes the F3 percentile from 8.42 to 8.45. The 'similar NDX path' condition, however, matches total return only. Requiring the actual rise-then-fall shape (NDX within 4pp of -4.0%, in-window peak at least +6%, drawdown at most -10%; 436 windows, 33 episodes) puts F3 at 17.4, F2 at 17.9 and the scanner version at 14.7. Since 2000 (279 windows, 22 episodes, about ±4pp sampling error) F3 ranks 3.6 and F2 7.2. Unconditionally since 2000, F3 ranks 6.9. The headline's 25th percentile is the most favourable of the conditional measures; the specialist's own NDX-regression residual gives 15.6. At lag 2 (Monday close, ranked against lag-2 history), F3 ranks 13.4.
verdicts.corrected: Unconditional F3 percentile 8.4 (6.9 since 2000; 13.4 at lag 2 against lag-2 history). Against windows with a similar NDX path (return within ±4pp, peak at least +6%, drawdown at most -10%): F3 17.4, F2 17.9 (1988+); F3 3.6, F2 7.2 (2000+, 22 episodes). Bad tail, still inside the historical range; normal only unconditionally.

verdicts.reason: Record-to-exit 10-07..10-16 is -16.38% (0.062nd percentile of 8-day windows). The held week is -13.88%; 4 of 1,944 weeks were worse (1995-07-21, 1996-03-01, 1999-07-23, 2007-03-02). The decision-time signatures check out: TQQQ/vol20/ER were 0.792/0.215/0.550, 0.850/0.100/0.375, 0.761/0.224/0.473 and 0.850/0.162/0.660, against 0.850/0.156/0.332 on 2026-10-09. F2's week was -9.39% (0.36th percentile). There is further support in-sample: 2026-06-05 lost -12.28% with the same signature (0.85/0.162/0.558). Weeks of -12% or worse occur 8 times in 38.8 years (about one every 4.9 years); 'once every 8 years' applies only to losses of 13.9% or more (5 events).

Decision-log weights reproduce: 37.3/35.9, Aug 16.2-21.2, Sep 21.2, 10-02 85.0. Average TQQQ weight freeze-to-record is 0.257, and TQQQ peaked +31.9% on 10-06. Rule-removal OOS: -9.0, -6.4, -1.4, +4.0. IS maxDD/Calmar: -30.0/0.80, -32.9/0.73, -46.6/0.60, -49.0/0.58. Record-to-exit is -16.4% in every variant. The drawdown benefit is not a 1990s artefact: from 2000 to the freeze, maxDD is -27.5% with both overlays vs -49.0% without (lag 2: -30.3% vs -56.5%).

Exit at the 10-16 close (NDX 29,188 < EMA 29,306), effective 10-19. Since then F3 and F2 are -0.93% while QQQ fell -7.45% and TQQQ -24.04%. No-gate counterfactual: F3 -22.79% (risk-off phase -15.95%, maxDD -32.59%), F2 -15.21%. Reproduced exactly; the gate mechanics match the independent engine.

The P&L numbers reproduce: F3 risk-on TQQQ -6.18, IEF -2.37, GLD +0.47, cost -0.06; scanner TQQQ -6.00, TLT -4.00, GLD +0.46; risk-off IEF +0.26, GLD -1.07; BIL off-leg -6.5% OOS, IS Calmar 0.72. The TLT-IEF gap is 1.85pp, not 1.86. The mechanism is wrong, though. All of IEF's loss came from 07-27 to 10-06 while NDX rose +11.0% (IEF -3.19%, TLT -6.06%; 10y yield 4.64% to 5.27%, peaking at 5.31% on 10-05). During the 10-07..10-16 crash, bonds rallied (IEF +1.45%, TLT +3.58%), but F3 held no bonds. Daily IEF-NDX correlation was +0.46 during the rally, so they did move together day to day, but their cumulative moves were opposite. This was not a 2022-style period where stocks and bonds both fell. The loss came from exposure timing: an average 0.59 IEF weight through the rally, then 85% TQQQ in the crash.
verdicts.corrected: Treasuries lost -2.37pp of capital while NDX rose +11% (yields 4.64% to 5.27%) and F3 was bond-heavy from the chop and Aug-Sep cuts. When stocks fell, bonds gained (IEF +1.45%, TLT +3.58%), but F3 held none. TLT cost 1.85pp more than IEF. Gold (-1.07pp) drove the loss after the exit.

verdicts.reason: Sleeve gaps reproduce: TQQQ -0.21pp (TE 2.16%/yr, expected 1-sigma 2.0pp), QLD +0.09, QQQ +0.18, IEF -0.17, TLT +0.05, BIL -0.05, GLD vs GC=F -0.02. Its effect is negligible: booking gold at month-end moves F3 IS by +0.03pp CAGR and +0.09pp maxDD, and the percentile by +0.03.

OOS F3: -8.99 / -7.49 / -5.90. The daily breakdown confirms it: open minus close is +3.47pp on 10-19 (TQQQ +4.10% overnight), with all other days summing to about -0.3pp. Lag 2 minus lag 1 is +3.36pp on 10-19 and -1.69pp on 10-05, and no other day exceeds 0.2pp. IS real-ETF drift reproduces (F3 25.7/-27.6/0.93, 24.8/-27.2/0.91, 26.3/-29.5/0.89; F2 0.78/0.76/0.77), as do the era CAGRs (34.5 vs 27.0, 11.4 vs 11.3, 25.1 vs 25.8) and full IS 24.13/0.80 vs 22.24/0.63. First, the 1988-99 edge has two sources: 1988-94 daily autocorrelation of +0.129 from a stale index (+5.8pp/yr), and in 1995-99 a few crash Mondays after Friday down-flips (+10.6pp/yr; 5 days give 0.323 of the 0.342 log gap, e.g. 1997-10-27 NDX -7.49%). Second, 'under 1pp/yr since 2010' holds for F3 and F2 only: Monday-open costs Strategy A 1.7pp/yr (maxDD -62.2% vs -59.3%) and the scanner version 1.2pp/yr.

Held 11-17: b and c are 85% IEF + 15% GLD, a is 85% TLT + 15% GLD, d is 100% BIL, decided 11-13; the 11-17 targets are identical. NDX 27,002 vs EMA 28,968.4 (-6.8%), vol 0.3551, ER 0.2597. Re-entry sizes: 0.85 x 0.20/0.355 = 47.9% TQQQ, 0.85 x 0.30/0.355 = 71.8% QLD, A 70.4%.

Numbers reproduce: A at the 51.7th percentile, worst week -16.08%, OOS DD -19.09%, IS -67.4%/0.45; F2 vs F3 -6.03 vs -8.99, DD -12.27 vs -17.35, weeks -9.39 vs -13.88, percentiles 9.1 vs 8.4, IS Calmar 0.82 vs 0.80. verdicts.corrected: A +6.9% is a median outcome. F2 vs F3 cannot be separated by this window. The in-sample Calmar near-tie (0.82 vs 0.80) is a 1990s effect: since 2000 F3 leads 0.72 vs 0.65 (model) and 0.93 vs 0.78 (real ETFs 2010-26). Any 2x preference rests on the cross-market tests.

issues: Reproducibility is exact. Re-executing oos_live.py with only its output path redirected gives 0 differing JSON leaves. A separate engine written without common.py matches every OOS and IS number to 0.001pp. No lookahead, splice, NaN/fillna(0), freeze-date or turnover-cost bug was found: real-ETF (PR) runs are used only inside the OOS window or after every ETF had launched (2010-02-19); the overnight-return data needed no fills; ETF and NDX calendars match 2010-2026; TQQQ/QQQ overnight correlation is 0.997 with slope 2.95.

F3's headline in-sample maxDD of -30.0% (Calmar 0.80) is set on 1990-05-02, inside the era C8 calls lag-1-flattered. At lag 2 it becomes -35.0% (1991-01-09), Calmar 0.63. From 2000 to the freeze: lag 1 gives 19.7% / -27.5% (2022-12-28) / 0.72, lag 2 gives 20.1% / -30.3% (2011-12-28) / 0.67. The key table's IS row should carry this caveat.

Headline wording: '25th percentile among windows with a similar NDX path' conditions on total return only. result.headline: No July conclusion is overturned by the 4 extra months or by the instrument correction. With IEF and GLD, F3 still shows an in-sample Calmar of 0.80 (0.79 to 2026-11-17), and all 9 July components help in both halves for both F2 and F3 (18/18). Walk-forward keeps the July defaults: re-tuned picks beat them in only 1 of 4 tests, at a selection cost of 0.04-0.16 Calmar. 2x is still preferred on risk-adjusted grounds: higher Sharpe in 108/108 paired configs in both halves, maxDD -24.0% vs -30.0%, OOS -6.0% vs -9.0%. 3x earns +4.3%/yr more CAGR, and that gap is statistically significant. The one material change is in implementation: the scanner's TLT off-leg drops F3 to Calmar 0.60 with a -40.7% maxDD. The defaults sit at the 96th-99th percentile of the parameter grid, so expect a forward Calmar nearer 0.7.

Keep the July rules and parameters exactly as they are. Re-tuning lost to the defaults in 3 of 4 walk-forward tests, the defaults sit on or near the parameter plateau, and selection cost is about 0.1 Calmar.

Make F2-IEF the primary strategy: QLD, vol target 0.30, chop threshold 0.25 with half size, half size in Aug-Sep, 15% physical gold (GLD), IEF as the off-leg. Vol target 0.25 is an equivalent alternative (Calmar 0.81, maxDD -23.7%).

Do not raise gold above 15% despite the in-sample gradient: the walk-forward picks with 25% gold did not beat the defaults in the test half. Do not drop the Aug-Sep rule over the 2026 OOS miss: its full-sample CAGR effect is zero and it consistently reduces drawdowns.

caveats: The out-of-sample window is only 81 trading days (2026-07-27..2026-11-17). That is far too short to rank anything; it is reported for transparency only.

The July defaults were chosen on all of 1988-2026 (with the proxy instruments), so their Calmar in each walk-forward test half is not truly out-of-sample. Only the walk-forward picks' test numbers are honest. The late-to-early walk-forward trains on 2007-01-01..2026-07-24 only, so no post-freeze data is used for any choice.

Physical gold before 2000-08-30 is monthly-interpolated: smoothed, and it uses the next month-end price. Gold's diversification benefit and volatility in 1988-2006 are therefore approximate. The series is used only as returns, never as a signal.

Calmar and max-drawdown differences on block-resampled paths are less reliable than CAGR differences. The IEF-vs-TLT Calmar gap is not significant in the bootstrap (P 0.71) and rests mostly on one regime, 2022.

With 2022 flattened, IEF still leads by +0.09 only because of 1989-10 to 1990-05 (synthetic TLT -34.8% vs IEF -30.0%). P(IEF has the better Calmar) is 0.70-0.80 for blocks of 21-252 days. The ~40% drawdown is one year (2022). IEF is a sensible duration hedge, but it is not a statistically robust 'material change'.
verdicts.corrected: TLT's -40.7% maxDD is the 2022 episode alone. Excluding 1989-90 and 2022, TLT beat IEF (1991-2006: 0.98 vs 0.89; 2007-2021: 1.10 vs 0.94). Gold minus IEF then gives: dCAGR +0.03%/yr (bootstrap P 0.52); maxDD -30.0% vs -30.5% (F3) and -24.0% vs -25.6% (F2), dMaxDD P 0.50; dCalmar +0.000 (F3, P 0.50) and -0.001 (F2, P 0.48). verdicts.corrected: Gold vs 15% IEF at the same 0.85 core: dCAGR +0.03%/yr (P 0.52), maxDD difference about 0 (P 0.50), full-sample bootstrap dCalmar about 0 (P 0.48-0.50). issues: Sharpe in common.py ignores the risk-free rate (July convention). That mechanically favours lower-exposure variants. Every Sharpe comparison across leverage levels should use excess returns: F2 minus F3 is P 0.99 raw but P 0.81 on excess returns.

The gold_w knob sets the leveraged core to 1 - gold_w, so in both the ablation and the grid gold is confounded with de-levering. At an equal core, gold vs IEF is about 0 on CAGR, maxDD and Calmar (bootstrap P about 0.5). The in-sample 'gold gradient' is largely a leverage gradient.

The walk-forward compares honest picks with defaults chosen on all of 1988-2026. Defaults average the 89th-92nd test percentile; honest picks the 45th-59th. That shows grid selection has no out-of-sample skill (so don't re-tune), not that the defaults are superior.

result.dimension: Off-leg policy for rising-rate / stocks-and-bonds-down regimes (KEY = rate_regime)
result.headline: No off-leg rule beats static IEF robustly. Every move to shorter-duration bonds or bills swaps protection in deflationary crashes for protection in inflationary ones. The best switch rule ('bond trend': hold BIL while IEF's total-return index is below its 200-day average) cuts 2022 from -22.1% to -13.0% and keeps most of the crash protection, but costs about 0.45%/yr, fails the both-halves test, and fails the bootstrap and Reality Check (p 0.86-0.99). Keep IEF and drop TLT. Today 4 of 6 rules say short duration, but in the selloff itself bonds have hedged (IEF +1.8% since the NDX record).

claims.claim: The baseline reproduces the audit exactly, so all comparisons use the audited mechanics. The off-leg is a big part of the portfolio: about 48% of capital on average (F3) and 85% whenever the gate is risk-off, which is 27% of days.

None of the 13 alternative off-legs (11 pre-specified plus 2 extras) meets the robustness bar in either strategy. The bar is: better than static IEF in both halves, by more than 0.07 Calmar, with bootstrap P(diff <= 0) < 0.10. On F3, nothing beats static IEF in-sample. On F2, four policies edge it on the full period, but each is worse in 1988-2006.
claims.evidence: F3 full-IS Calmar: IEF 0.80; durA, durB and bond trend 0.79; corr63, 50/50, thirds and inflation 0.77; corr126 0.76; SHY 0.76; bills 0.72; TLT 0.60. F2: bond trend 0.89, 50/50 0.84, corr126 0.84, inflation 0.83 vs IEF 0.82. But F2 H1 (1988-2006) Calmar: bond trend 0.92, 50/50 0.87, corr126 0.85, inflation 0.85, all below IEF's 0.96. The 'robust' flag is False for all 26 strategy-policy pairs.

claims.claim: The statistical tests reject any edge. Every move to shorter duration lowers CAGR. Calmar confidence intervals all straddle zero, and the selection-adjusted Reality Check finds nothing.
claims.evidence: Paired block bootstrap (2000 draws, 63-day blocks, IS). CAGR difference vs IEF for F3: bills -2.09%/yr [-3.72, -0.49]; 50/50 -1.02 [-1.85, -0.22]; durA -1.01 [-2.05, +0.06]; bond trend -0.43 [-1.23, +0.41]; TLT +0.25 [-1.31, +1.84]. P(Calmar diff <= 0) ranges 0.61-0.91. P(Calmar diff > 0.07) for bond trend: 3.0% (F3), 7.6% (F2). White's Reality Check p-values: 12 main policies 0.90 (F3) / 0.86 (F2); whole 25-policy pool 0.94 / 0.92; switch rules only 0.98 / 0.99, and the best switch rule's mean log-return difference is negative (-0.33%/yr F3, -0.37%/yr F2).

claims.claim: Walk-forward selection adds nothing, and the rankings flip between halves. Picking on 1988-2006 chooses static IEF. Picking on 2007-2026 chooses bond trend, which then loses to IEF in 1988-2006.
claims.evidence: Pick on H1, test on H2: static IEF chosen in both strategies; it ranks 5/12 in H2 for F3 (0.88) and 9/12 for F2 (0.77). Pick on H2, test on H1: bond trend chosen; H1 Calmar 0.77 vs IEF 0.80 (F3) and 0.92 vs 0.96 (F2). Rank correlation of Calmar between halves: 0.35 (F3), 0.56 (F2). Re-picking every year on all data so far, 1996 to 2026-07: realised Calmar 0.88 vs static IEF 0.89 (F3) and 0.83 vs 0.84 (F2). Selection cost measured in this family: 0.07 Calmar for F2 (hindsight bond trend 0.91 vs walk-forward 0.83), about 0.01 for F3.

claims.claim: The trade-off is structural. A month-by-month breakdown shows short duration gains when stocks and bonds fall together and loses in flight-to-quality months. Bond trend has the best shape: it costs nothing when rates are falling and pays for itself only through whipsaw and lost yield when rates are flat.
claims.evidence: F3, IS months, sum of log excess return vs static IEF. Static bills: +73% in stocks-down/bonds-down months (77 months), -104% in stocks-down/bonds-up (105), -104% in both-up (172). Bond trend: +23%, -11% and -36% in the same buckets; by 6-month 10y change, +16.5% when rates rose 50bp+ (90 months), -29.7% when flat (259), 0.0% when they fell 50bp+ (113). Net about -0.34%/yr. durA loses -56.5% in flat-rate months.

claims.claim: Crisis table, F3 in-sample. Inflationary bears (1994, 2022) improve sharply with short duration. Deflationary crashes get worse with bills or durA, but not with bond trend, because bonds are usually trending up during deflationary crashes.
claims.evidence: 2022: IEF -22.1%; bills/durA -12.1%; bond trend -13.0%; 50/50 -17.2%; corr63 -21.3%. 1994: IEF -6.3%; bills/durA -1.2%; bond trend -1.4%. Dot-com: IEF +2.3%; bills -15.5%; durA -7.4%; inflation rule -10.8%; bond trend +0.4%. GFC: IEF +4.0%; bills -9.1%; durA -4.5%; bond trend +3.6%. COVID: IEF -11.6%, bills -15.4%, switch rules -11.6%. 1998: IEF +9.7%, bills +4.4%. Underlying instruments: 2022 IEF -15.2%, TLT -31.2%, bills +1.4%; dot-com IEF +38.7%; GFC IEF +22.3%.

claims.claim: Calmar is decided by a single worst drawdown. F3's worst is 1989-90, so fixing 2022 just exposes 2011 and full-period Calmar doesn't move. F2's worst IS 2022, so bond trend lifts F2 to Calmar 0.89 and beats an equal-drawdown cash dial by about 1.1%/yr. That gain comes from one episode and does not appear in 1988-2006.
claims.evidence: F3 + IEF max drawdown: -30.0% (1989-10-09 to 1990-05-02); its H2 worst is -27.5% (2021-11 to 2022-12). With bond trend the H2 worst becomes 2011 at -26.3%. F2 + IEF max drawdown: -24.0% (2021-11-19 to 2022-12-28); bond trend's is -21.7% (2000-03 to 2000-09). Cash dial (blend of static-IEF strategy and BIL) at the same -21.7%: 18.18% CAGR vs bond trend 19.27%. Lowering the vol target (F2 0.24-0.28, F3 0.16-0.19) only moves maxDD by about 0.5pp, so it cannot match.

claims.claim: TLT, which the live scanner currently recommends, is confirmed as the worst off-leg on risk. Its small CAGR edge is noise.
claims.evidence: F3 TLT: maxDD -40.7% vs -30.0%, Calmar 0.60 vs 0.80, H2 Calmar 0.59 vs 0.88, 2022 -33.9%. F2 TLT: Calmar 0.53 vs 0.82, maxDD -37.5%. Bootstrap CAGR difference +0.25%/yr [-1.31, +1.84].

claims.claim: OOS (not used for any selection): the short-duration rules lost about 2.5pp less, but all of that gap came while stocks were rising and bonds falling (Jul 25 to Oct 6). In the selloff since the NDX record, bonds hedged. The current episode is not a 2022-type stocks-and-bonds-down regime so far.
claims.evidence: Full OOS, F3: bills/durA/corr126/bond trend -6.5% vs IEF -9.0%; F2: -3.5% vs -6.0%. Jul 25 to Oct 6: NDX +11.0%, IEF -3.2%, 10y +59bp; F3 bills +12.8% vs IEF +9.9%. Oct 7 to Nov 17: NDX -13.5%, IEF +1.8%, TLT +3.4%, 10y -17bp; every policy -17.2%. Since risk-off took effect (Oct 19): IEF +0.33%, bills +0.32%, both policies -0.9%; the loss is gold at -7.7%. Only Nov 6-17 saw yields up 27bp (IEF -1.7%), and NDX rose 1.4% in that stretch.

claims.claim: What each rule says today. The strategy is risk-off, so 85% sits in the off-leg plus 15% gold. Four of the six pre-specified rules say short duration; the 63-day correlation rule and the inflation rule say IEF.
claims.evidence: Data to 2026-11-17; last weekly decision 2026-11-13. durA: bills (10y 5.10% vs its 200-day average 4.59%, +51bp; since 2026-03-11). durB: SHY. corr63: IEF (correlation -0.14; flipped 2026-10-30). corr126: bills (+0.10; since 2026-03-26). Bond trend: bills (IEF 1.8% below its 200-day average; since 2026-06-30). Inflation: IEF (GSCI 3.8% below its 200-day average, though up 20% over 12 months; flipped 2026-11-09). Target today: 85% IEF + 15% GLD (static) vs 85% BIL + 15% GLD (short rules).

claims.claim: Parameter sensitivity: bond trend is a stable plateau, not a lucky setting, but every setting still loses to IEF in 1988-2006 on F2. durA, corr and inflation results swing with their parameters.
claims.evidence: Bond-trend average length 100/150/200/250/300 days, plus one extra week of delay. F2 Calmar 0.89, 0.88, 0.89, 0.90, 0.89, delayed 0.90; H1 0.92-0.94 vs IEF 0.96. F3 0.84, 0.81, 0.79, 0.81, 0.80, delayed 0.82. durA (F3) dot-com result ranges -5.8% to -12.8%; corr window 42/252 days gives F2 Calmar 0.74/0.83; inflation-rule length 100/300 gives 0.75/0.74.

claims.claim: Positioning risk right now: with 85% in IEF, each 50bp move in the 10y yield is worth about 3% of the portfolio either way. IEF's extra yield over bills is under 1%/yr.

result.current_read: As of 2026-11-17 the strategy is risk-off (NDX below its EMA-100 since the 2026-10-16 weekly decision). So the off-leg holds 85% of capital, with 15% in gold, and this choice matters right now. Static IEF says IEF. Four of the six pre-specified switch rules say short duration: durA bills, durB SHY, corr126 bills, bond trend bills. The 63-day correlation rule (-0.14) and the inflation rule say IEF. The 10y yield is 5.10%, 51bp above its 200-day average, and IEF is 1.8% below its 200-day average. The walk-forward currently holds IEF for F3 and bills for F2. The OOS evidence does not show a 2022-style regime: since the NDX record on Oct 6, IEF is +1.8% and TLT +3.4% while NDX fell 13.5%. Since risk-off took effect, IEF and bills are level (+0.3%), and the strategy's loss comes from gold (-7.7%). The short-duration rules' 2.5pp OOS lead was earned while stocks were rallying (Jul 25 to Oct 6), not in the selloff.
result.recommendation:
Keep static IEF as the off-leg for both F3 and F2. Change the scanner from TLT to IEF: TLT is the worst policy on risk (F3 Calmar 0.60, maxDD -40.7%, 2022 -33.9%).

Do not adopt any duration-switch rule as an improvement. None survives the both-halves test, the bootstrap (P(Calmar gain > 0.07) at most 7.6%), the Reality Check (p 0.86-0.99) or the walk-forward (yearly re-picking 0.88/0.83 vs static 0.89/0.84). The measured selection cost in this family is about 0.07 Calmar, which is larger than the best rule's 0.07 in-sample gain.

If the user still wants explicit insurance against a 2022 repeat, given a 5% 10y yield in an uptrend, the only acceptable rule is bond trend (hold BIL while IEF's total-return index is below its 200-day average). Treat it as a paid hedge, not an edge. It costs about 0.45%/yr long-run (about 0.9%/yr in a 1988-2006-type falling-rate world), cuts 2022 from -22% to -13% and 1994 from -6% to -1%, and keeps nearly all dot-com and GFC protection. For F2 only, it beats an equal-drawdown cash dial by about 1.1%/yr, but all of that comes from 2022. A static 50/50 IEF/BIL split is the parameter-free middle ground (F2 Calmar 0.84, about -1%/yr CAGR).

Today the choice is a judgment call worth about 3% of the portfolio per 50bp move in the 10y yield. Don't let the 16-week OOS result drive it.
caveats: The sample has only two inflationary bear markets (1994, 2022), so any rule that 'fixes' them is effectively fitted to two data points; F2's full-period Calmar gain comes entirely from 2022.

Calmar depends on a single worst drawdown, so it can jump when one episode changes. That is why the bootstrap's mean Calmar difference for F2 bond trend (-0.01) disagrees with the in-sample point estimate (+0.07).

Before 2002-07-30, IEF, SHY and TLT are synthetic: calibrated on yields and fitted to the real ETFs (IEF tracking error 2.2%/yr, correlation 0.95). Bills before 2007-05 are the 3-month T-bill rate minus fees. The correlation and bond-trend signals before 2002 therefore run on synthetic IEF, which is causal (built only from yields) but approximate.

Gold before 2000-08 is monthly-interpolated and uses future month-end prices. It is held identically in every policy and drives no signal, so it does not bias the comparison, but it understates early-period volatility.

The OOS window is about 16 weeks and was never used for selection; its policy ranking is anecdotal. In detail it is not a stocks-and-bonds-down episode: bonds fell while stocks rose, then hedged during the selloff.
The inflation rule uses the GSCI level from data_letf/geo_panel (assumed to be the S&P GSCI price index); results depend on that series.

Mechanics are common.py's: Friday decisions, lag=1, 3bp costs. Switching between IEF and bills is charged turnover, but the different ETF fees are only reflected after each ETF's inception (2002 for IEF, 2007 for BIL).

issues: Reproducibility is clean. I re-ran rate_regime.py unchanged with output sent to scratch: none of the numeric leaves differ from rate_regime.json. A separate re-implementation matches to 5e-7. I found no look-ahead in the switch signals: all use trailing windows, a Friday mark and lag=1. The variant count of 98 is correct (24+24+12+4+4+8+22).

The robustness bar has almost no power on its bootstrap leg. For any off-leg change, resampling pulls the mean Calmar difference to about -0.007, even where the in-sample difference is +0.063. The same bootstrap cannot separate TLT from IEF: P(TLT Calmar <= IEF) is 0.70 (F3) and 0.80 (F2). So 'fails the bootstrap' tells us little either way. The 'no robust edge' verdict is still supported by evidence that does have power: the both-halves test, leave-one-episode-out, and rolling 5-year windows (bond trend beats IEF on Calmar in only 38% (F3) and 34% (F2) of 68 windows, and on CAGR in 28%).

The specialist's Reality Check uses mean daily log return, which mechanically favours longer duration and so cannot credit a defensive rule. I re-ran it on Sharpe and Calmar over the 12 main policies and the conclusion holds. On Sharpe, IEF is best for both strategies (p 0.999). On Calmar, F2's best is +0.063 with p 0.46. Restricted to the bond-trend family on F2, p is 0.13 with re-centring on the bootstrap mean. With White re-centring on the observed value it is 0.03, but that is inflated because Calmar is biased under resampling, so it is not reliable evidence.

The quoted cost of the bond-trend hedge, about 0.45%/yr, is optimistic. It is the cheapest of the 6 pre-specified rule types (the average of the 6 is -0.78%/yr on F3 and -0.80%/yr on F2). On post-2022 real data, 2023-01 to 2026-07-24 (high, range-bound rates like today), bond trend cost -4.1% (F3) and -4.5% (F2) log vs IEF, about 1.2%/yr. durA lost -6.5% / -7.2% and corr126 -4.6% / -5.0%. The OOS recovered only +2.7pp, so bond trend is still -1.5% / -1.8% log behind IEF since 2023. The F2 walk-forward's switch to bond trend after 2022 lost -4.5% log up to the freeze.

In the real-ETF era, the whole ranking hinges on 2022. From 2002-08 to 2026-07 including 2022, bond trend beats IEF (F3 0.814 vs 0.801; F2 0.816 vs 0.715) and 7 of 11 alternatives beat IEF on F2. With 2022 neutralised in both series, IEF beats bond trend (0.877 vs 0.841; 0.884 vs 0.846), and only TLT beats IEF, in both strategies.

F3's 'nothing beats IEF' depends on pre-1996 synthetic data. F3's IS Calmar is pinned by two drawdowns both policies share, 1989-90 (-30.0%) and 1995-96 (-29.2%), in the era of synthetic TQQQ and IEF and monthly-interpolated gold. From a 1996 start, bond trend (0.901) and corr126 (0.908) beat IEF (0.892). The margins are below 0.07, so the verdict stands, but the claimed F3 cost should be read in that light.

Drawdown measures that are not one number: over the full IS period, bond trend has the lowest Ulcer index (12.35 vs IEF 12.50 on F3; 8.68 vs 8.83 on F2), and the Martin ratio is a tie (1.92 vs 1.93; 2.22 vs 2.23). By decade, bond trend's Calmar wins only in the 2020s, and its CAGR is lower in 4 of 5 decades (F3: -1.43, -0.27, -1.25, -0.49, +1.36 %/yr). This supports 'a wash at best'.

Minor: the synthetic IEF, TLT and SHY (alpha, duration, convexity) were calibrated on 2002-2026 real ETF data and then applied to pre-2002 yields. That is a small look-ahead in how the instruments were built. All policies share it, and its effect on the bond-trend signal is negligible (the drift is about 0.3%/yr). But H1, where every candidate fails the both-halves test, sits entirely in this synthetic era.

result.headline: Managed-futures (TSMOM) sleeve does NOT pass: 0 of 24 pre-specified F2/F3 structures beat the baseline by more than the 0.15-Calmar selection cost with a significant bootstrap. Swapping the IEF off-leg for TSMOM fixes 2022 (F3 -22.1% -> -4.6%) but LOWERS 1988-2026 Calmar in 22/22 proxy variants (F3 0.80 -> 0.73); permanent 10-30% sleeves are mostly plain de-levering (a same-size T-bill sleeve does about as well on Calmar).

claims.claim: Baselines reproduce the audit exactly, and no TSMOM structure passes the anti-overfitting bar (dCalmar > 0.15, positive in both halves, paired block-bootstrap 95% CI excluding 0).
claims.evidence: IS 1988-01-01..2026-07-24: F3+GLD+IEF 24.13%/-30.0%/Calmar 0.80/2022 -22.1%; F2+GLD+IEF 19.71%/-24.0%/0.82/Sharpe 1.03. Main grid (12m and 1/3/12m blend proxies x 6 structures x F2/F3 = 24): 0 PASS, 5 MARGINAL (all F2 permanent sleeves), 19 FAIL. Best dCalmar +0.10 (F2 20% blend sleeve, CI [-0.04,+0.21]). In the 252-row robustness grid (21 proxy variants x 12) no TSMOM row exceeds +0.15 dCalmar (max +0.15, F2 30% sleeve).

claims.claim: Replacing IEF with TSMOM as the off-leg (the intuitive 2022 fix) improves 2022 and CAGR but worsens full-history drawdown and Calmar, robustly across all proxy variants.

Mechanism: in F's risk-off state (where the off-leg matters) TSMOM earns no more than IEF; its edge comes while F is already risk-on, largely by being long the same equity trend. It is not a reliable stocks-and-bonds-down hedge month to month.
claims.evidence: IS annualised excess return over T-bills, F risk-off days (2,644): proxy 5.3%/yr vs IEF 5.6%/yr (proxy vol ~12.7% vs IEF ~6.5%); F risk-on days (7,068): proxy 10.3% vs IEF 1.9%. Proxy daily corr with F3 baseline 0.30. In 69 IS months with SPX<0 and IEF<0, proxy averaged -0.73%/month (IEF -1.67%) and beat T-bills only 42% of the time.

claims.claim: Permanent TSMOM sleeves mostly reproduce plain de-levering; against a same-size T-bill sleeve they add return but not a robust Calmar gain, and almost no extra 2022 or OOS protection.
claims.evidence: T-bill sleeve 10/20/30% dCalmar vs baseline: F3 +0.02/+0.04/+0.07, F2 +0.01/+0.03/+0.05. TSMOM sleeve minus T-bill sleeve (IS): Calmar F3 -0.01/-0.04/-0.07; F2 +0.07/+0.04/+0.00 with H1 -0.03/-0.08/-0.15; CAGR +1.0/+2.0/+2.9%/yr (CIs exclude 0); rf-adjusted Sharpe +0.02 to +0.09; 2022 only +1.1/+2.2/+3.4pp; OOS +0.0pp.

claims.claim: Versus the baseline (not vs cash), sleeves give statistically significant Sharpe gains and shallower maxDD but cost CAGR; the Calmar gain is not significant.
claims.evidence: F2 +20% main: Calmar 0.82->0.90, maxDD -24.0->-20.6%, CAGR -1.29%/yr, dSharpe (rf-ignoring, as July) +0.087 CI [+0.039,+0.138], dCalmar CI [-0.03,+0.24]. F3 +20%: Calmar 0.80->0.81, CAGR -2.0%/yr CI [-4.14,-0.13]. Part of the Sharpe gain is mechanical because C.stats ignores rf: a 20% T-bill sleeve alone moves F2 Sharpe 1.03->1.06.

claims.claim: Proxy fidelity to real managed-futures ETFs is moderate. The proxy is more equity-heavy and under-captures 2022, so it understates real CTAs' diversification in the recent window.

claims.claim: The proxy's 38-year standalone return is mostly secular bond/equity beta, not trend timing; timing mainly changes crisis behaviour.
claims.evidence: Always-long control (same 8 markets, sizing, 12% scaling, costs): IS excess Sharpe 0.73 vs TSMOM 0.70 (H1 0.61 vs 0.77; H2 0.84 vs 0.64). 2022 -17.4% vs +13.9%; OOS -5.2% vs +0.9%. Dividends added back 0.82; GSG commodity leg from 2006: 0.66; gold-miners pre-2000 signal 0.75; realised-vol scaling 0.70. 2022 ranges from +5.6% (drop IEF) to +27.9% (ex-equities).

claims.claim: The 2019-2026 real-ETF evidence is a recency trap: on DBMF's live window the off-leg swap looks excellent with real DBMF and with the proxy alike, but the 38-year history reverses it.

Proxy over the same window: 1.47 / 1.54. 20% real-DBMF sleeve: F3 +0.15, F2 +0.33. KMLM off-leg on its window: +0.13 both. Full 1988-2026 with the proxy: off-leg swap dCalmar -0.07 / -0.06 (C2).

claims.claim: The most economically motivated alternative, ex-equity TSMOM (KMLM-like, avoids doubling the Nasdaq trend), is the closest to passing but still fails. It was picked after seeing results, so it carries selection cost.
claims.evidence: F2 + 20% ex-equity sleeve IS 18.1%/-19.0%/Calmar 0.95 (H1 1.04, H2 1.04), dCalmar +0.13, bootstrap CI [-0.02,+0.28], 2022 -12.0%, OOS -3.9%. F3 +20%: dCalmar +0.04, CI [-0.01,+0.21]. Off-leg replacement still negative: F2 -0.02, F3 -0.06.

Blend 1/3/12m: equities -1/3 each (NDX 1m -8.9%, 3m -9.1%), IEF/TLT -1/3, gold -1, DXY +1/3 held (+1 live), GSCI +1 held (-1/3 live, 1m -10.5%).

result.current_read: The strategy is risk-off, so the IEF off-leg plus 15% gold applies; nothing in this dimension argues for changing that. The 12m TSMOM proxy, held since the 2026-10-30 rebalance (scale 0.24, gross 2.86x NAV), is LONG SPX/NDX/intl equities (12m excess still +5.0/+4.0/+9.1%). It is SHORT IEF/TLT (-6.0/-9.7%) and SHORT gold (-9.7%), and LONG the dollar (+4.3%) and GSCI commodities (+20.0%). It therefore disagrees with F's EMA-100 risk-off on equities. The faster 1/3/12m blend is already net short equities, bonds and gold, long USD, and is flipping commodities to short. Since the freeze the proxy made +0.9% (DBMF +2.5%, KMLM -0.3%, T-bills ~+1.2%). A 20% TSMOM sleeve would have cut F3's OOS loss from -9.0% to -6.9%, exactly what a 20% T-bill sleeve did.
result.recommendation: Do not add a managed-futures sleeve to the live strategy; keep F's IEF off-leg and the permanent 15% physical gold. (1) Do not replace IEF with a DBMF/KMLM-type TSMOM fund: it fixes 2022 (-22% -> -5%) but lowers 1988-2026 Calmar in 22/22 variants because 1989-90, 1994, 2011 and 2018-Q4 get worse. The attractive 2019-2026 real-DBMF result is a single-regime (2022) sample. (2) Do not replace gold with TSMOM. (3) A permanent 10-20% sleeve is mostly de-levering. If a lower-drawdown F2 is wanted for 2022-type regimes, an extra 10-20% in T-bills/short Treasuries gives most of the same Calmar and 2022 benefit with no model risk. A TSMOM sleeve adds ~1-2%/yr of return over cash but no robust Calmar gain (negative in 1988-2006); in F3 it is no better than holding cash. Revisit only if a long, faithful CTA index history (monthly, from about 1990) can be obtained to re-test the off-leg swap with a real product rather than this 8-market proxy.
caveats: The proxy is a coarse 8-market TSMOM: 3 highly correlated equity legs, 2 bond legs, no short-rate futures, no individual FX pairs or commodities. It fits real DBMF/KMLM only moderately (weekly corr 0.61/0.37) and cannot be validated before 2019. Real diversified CTAs likely had shallower losses than the proxy in 1994 (-16.2%), 2016 (-22.0%) and 2018 (-13.6%), but no CTA index data is in the panel to check this.

Data approximations: gsci is the S&P GSCI SPOT index with no roll yield (2022 spot +8.7% vs futures-based GSG +24.1%); DXY FX carry is omitted; spx/ndx/intl are price indices with no dividends. Sensitivities (GSG commodity leg from 2006, constant dividend add-back, both combined) did not change any verdict.

Gold before 2000-09 is a log-interpolated monthly-average series. Signals were lagged 21 trading days; gold vol used 36m of monthly returns lagged one month, divided by the 0.774 smoothing ratio from panel_validation.json; gold was excluded from the ex-ante risk window until 126 real daily observations existed (2001-03-05). Pre-2000 gold P&L is therefore smoothed.
The common C.stats Sharpe ignores rf (as in July), which mechanically flatters cash-like sleeves; rf-adjusted Sharpe is reported for the controls and the TSMOM-vs-cash comparison.

The bootstrap is a paired circular block bootstrap (63-day blocks, 2000 draws, in-sample only, seed 0); it reproduces common.block_bootstrap_cagr_diff exactly for CAGR. Drawdown/Calmar statistics on resampled paths are indicative only.

319 variants were evaluated (23 proxy constructions and 296 portfolios: 24 main-grid, 252 robustness re-runs incl. 12 always-long control rows, 6 T-bill controls, 12 real-ETF window checks, 2 baselines). Robustness rows were pre-declared and not used for selection, but any best-looking row (e.g. ex-equities) still carries selection cost.
The OOS window is only ~4 months (2026-07-25..2026-11-17) and supports no inference; nothing was chosen using it.

Implementation: DBMF/KMLM are US-domiciled ETFs. Given the stated preference for UCITS above $60k, a UCITS managed-futures equivalent and its tracking would need checking separately if this were ever adopted.

result.headline: No macro overlay deserves inclusion. The July 'confirmed yield-curve' rule never changes a position, and all of its claimed +1.0%/yr came from holding bonds instead of cash in the off-leg. All 54 genuine overlay variants were rejected (curve, rate shock, dollar, credit, VIX term structure; 0 included, 0 marginal). The only real signal is a 6-month dollar surge, and it is too small to use (Calmar +0.005 on F3, +0.06 on F2, mostly from 1988-2006). Today the trend gate is off, so no overlay changes current holdings.

claims.claim: The July 'confirmed yield-curve' rule is a logical no-op. It never changes a position in the backtest or in scanner.py, which uses the same expression.
claims.evidence: Algebra: A and not(I and not A) = A (absorption law). Truth table: risk_on equals 'above' in all 4 rows. On the panel the 'confirmed' flag was ON on 734 of 10,362 days, but every one of those days was already risk-off, so it changed risk-on on 0 days. F3 and F2 backtests with the rule on vs off: max |daily return difference| = 0.0 and max weight difference = 0. The rule had no effect in any of the 8 cells of the 2x2 grid (off-leg x rule on/off).

claims.claim: The July '+1.0%/yr curve edge' was 100% the bond off-leg. Exact reproduction on the archived July inputs with frontier.py mechanics.
claims.evidence: vol25 with cash off-leg: 31.64% / -67.3% / Calmar 0.470; adding the confirmed rule leaves it identical. vol25 with bond off-leg and no rule: 32.14% / -64.6% / 0.497, identical to the July 'curve:confirm' row in frontier.csv (0.321409 / -0.646101 / 0.4975). Edge vs the cash dial: +0.995%/yr = rule +0.000 + bond off-leg +0.995. The genuine raw-inversion rule (July 'curve:raw') cost 2.14% CAGR vs bond-only (30.00% vs 32.14%).

claims.claim: On the corrected panel (in-sample to 2026-07-24), the off-leg choice matters; the curve rule does not.
claims.evidence: F3, cash (BIL) off-leg: 22.06% / -30.5% / Calmar 0.722. With IEF: 24.13% / -30.0% / 0.805 (+2.07%/yr; halves 0.69->0.80 and 0.79->0.88). Benefit: dot-com +2.3% with IEF vs -15.5% with cash.

claims.claim: Genuine curve rules all fail. They are slightly negative overall and depend on only 3-4 episodes.
claims.evidence: Inversion caps the engine at 0.5: F3 Calmar 0.785 vs 0.805 (-0.020), F2 -0.008. Inversion -> risk-off (the July raw rule): F3 -0.059, F2 -0.044. result.recommendation:
Do not add any macro overlay to F2 or F3.

1. Delete the 'confirmed yield-curve' clause from the rulebook and scanner.py as dead code. It provably never changes a position. Re-label the July '+1%/yr curve gain' as the bond off-leg gain.
2. Keep IEF, not cash and not TLT, as the off-leg.
3. Do not adopt the rate-shock x0.5 rule even though it would have cut the out-of-sample loss (F3 -9.0% -> -1.6%). In-sample it is negative in both halves, so adopting it would mean choosing a parameter from post-freeze data.
4. The rate-shock -> bills off-leg is a regime bet like the July duration switch: 2022 better by +4 to +8pp, 1988-2006 worse. It is a judgement call about the inflation regime, not a validated improvement.
5. Put the 6-month dollar-surge de-risk (DXY up more than 5% in 126 days -> engine x0.75) on a watch-list only. Its Sharpe gain is real (placebo p 0.005 or lower) but small, below the haircut, and absent in 2007-2026. Re-test it once roughly 2-3 more years of genuinely out-of-sample data exist, or on other markets, before using it.
caveats: The macro event count is tiny. Only 3 un-inversion episodes qualify (2001, 2007, 2024-26), or 4 with the alternative definition (adds 2019-21). Curve, rate-shock and dollar results are each driven by a handful of episodes, so statistical power is low in both directions.

The un-inversion rule needed an interpretation. I measured 'within 24 months' from the last day of a contiguous inverted spell of at least 63 days. In 2019 no spell reached 63 contiguous days (18/12/31/18), so that year only triggers under the alternative cumulative-count definition (>=63 inverted days in 252), which was also tested.

The credit ETF window (2008+) and the VIX3M window (2006+) are about 18-20 years, and the baseline Calmar on those windows is higher (F3 0.955 and 0.890). For these, the 'halves' are the window split at its midpoint, not 1988-2006 vs 2007+.

FRED (Moody's BAA/AAA, HY OAS) was unreachable from this machine (connection reset / timeout), so there is no Moody's-spread test. The long-history credit proxy is the VWEHX mutual-fund NAV (about 40% zero-return days from cent rounding), used only as a 50/200-day trend signal; its flags agree with HYG/IEF 93% of the time from 2007.
Every macro input was lagged one extra trading day on top of the engine's one-day weight lag. This is conservative; slightly faster use of the signals could change the results marginally.
The baselines' 15% static gold sleeve before 2000-08-30 uses monthly-interpolated gold, which contains look-ahead. No overlay signal uses gold, and the effect is common to all variants.

Bootstrap p-values (circular blocks of 63 days, 2,000 resamples) are per test and not corrected for multiple testing. F2 and F3 are highly correlated, so the 54 variants amount to roughly 27 independent tests. The dollar-shock p-values (0.001-0.006) survive a rough Bonferroni correction only for F2.
The OOS window is only 82 trading days, so OOS differences (e.g. rate shock +5.9 to +7.4pp) are anecdotal and were not used for any decision.
External series (HYG, IEF, LQD, VWEHX, ^VIX, ^VIX3M) were fetched from yfinance on 2026-11-18 and cached in update_2026_11/overlays_ext.parquet so reruns are deterministic.

result.current_read:
These are in-sample conditional base rates, not a forecast.

**Where we are (out-of-sample).** The strategy is risk-off: 85% IEF and 15% gold since the 2026-10-16 mark. Since then it is down 0.9% while NDX is down 7.5%. The weekly rule ignored 2 short daily re-crosses above the EMA.

**What followed similar states, 1988 to 2026-07-24 (29 unique episodes):**
- **NDX:** median +7% at 3 months and +21% at 12 months; higher after 12 months in 82%.
- **Bear markets:** about 29% went on to a fall of more than 25% from the 52-week peak within 12 months (95% CI 15-47%).
- **Re-entry:** the strategy re-entered after a median 21 trading days (IQR 10-44). About 1 in 5 episodes stayed risk-off for more than 3 months.
- **Whipsaws:** about 60% had at least one re-entry that was reversed within 6 months.
- **Strategy returns:** F2-IEF and F3-IEF were positive over 12 months in 96% of episodes, with medians of +16% and +18%. That is about QQQ's +22% median, but with a far smaller worst case (-11% vs -62%).
- **The only strategy loss:** the 2022 stocks-and-bonds-down episode, when IEF fell 10% and TLT 23% over 12 months.

**Bootstrap from risk-off starts:** 12-month median +18% for F2 and +22% for F3. Loss probabilities are 12% and 14%, against 15% and 18% unconditional. QQQ has a 27% loss probability and a -31% 5th percentile.

**What doesn't match:** today's macro mix has no close analog. Gold is down 15% in 63 days (a 1-in-100 move), and yields and the dollar are rising at the same time.
result.recommendation:
The analog evidence does not justify any rule change.

1. **Conditioning adds no information.** The analog-set medians sit within the 26th to 94th percentile of random risk-off sets. The strategy's 12-month distribution from a risk-off start is about the same as unconditional, with a thinner left tail. No parameter was chosen from post-freeze data, and none should be.
2. **Use the base rates to set expectations.** Typical waits are 1-2 months, but 21% lasted more than 3 months. A quick re-entry that reverses happened in about 60% of episodes; that is normal behaviour, not a broken signal. The median cost of waiting was about 2-3% of NDX upside.
3. **The live exposure is the bond off-leg, not the equity timing.** The only negative 12-month outcome in any analog set was the 2022 rates-up bear. Today the 10y is up 44bp over 126 days and the portfolio is 85% IEF, so the off-leg duration choice is what matters now (that question belongs to the rates-regime workstream).
4. **The live scanner holds TLT, not IEF.** In the analogs TLT had the worse record: 12-month minimum -23.4% and 75% positive, against -10.2% and 79% for IEF. The scanner and backtest should hold the same bond leg; IEF is the one with the better record.
5. **F2 vs F3.** F3's analog medians are higher, but F2's drawdowns are smaller (12-month max DD median -11.3% vs -15.8%). That is consistent with the earlier finding that 2x is better on a risk-adjusted basis.
caveats: Small samples: 8-21 episodes per set and 28 unique episodes with a full 12-month window. The 82% NDX hit rate has a Wilson 95% interval of 64-92%, and the 29% bear-market rate an interval of 15-47%. Medians move by about 10pp between sets.

The sets overlap heavily and are not independent confirmations. The 2022-01/02 and 2018-10/11 clusters appear in 8 of 9 sets. Episodes inside one bear market (2022-01, 2022-04 and 2022-09; 2007-11 and 2008-07) are dependent.

The brief's ATH-based rule (R1) silently drops 2001-2014, because the 2000 high was not regained until about 2015-17. Half of R1's episodes are 1990-1998 bull-market dips. R2 (DD from the 52-week high) fixes this and gives lower strategy medians (F3 +22.4% vs +34.0%).

The in-sample period is mostly a secular bond bull market (1988-2020), which flatters the IEF off-leg: IEF's 12-month median in the analogs is +6.7%. 2022 is the only close rates-up bear analog, so off-leg results may not transfer to a regime with 5%+ and rising yields.

Today's macro combination has no close analog. Gold -14.8% over 63 days is the 0.9th percentile, and rising yields plus a rising dollar come with it. The nearest K3 match is about 0.5x the median candidate distance, versus 0.08x for the price-only K1.

Simulated history before inception: QQQ before 1999, QLD before 2006, TQQQ before 2010, and IEF/TLT before 2002-07 (calibrated synthetic). Gold before 2000-08 is monthly-interpolated: it is used only as a return sleeve, and gold signals are computed only from 2000-12 on.

The bootstrap breaks dependence beyond 63-day blocks, and the state matching keeps only on/off persistence. The first-block pools are clustered: B3 draws its 301 days from about 54 runs, and B4 its 768 days from about 75. The empirical risk-off distribution (F3 loss in 5% of 12-month windows) uses overlapping windows from about 95 risk-off spells.

All analog outcomes stop at the 2026-07-24 freeze. The 2026-03-26/31 analogs in K2 and K3 have no 6- or 12-month outcome. Today's state is out-of-sample and used only as the query; no parameter was chosen.

Variant count is 19: the 9 analog sets, the union, 5 bootstrap schemes and 3 empirical conditionings, plus a first R1a definition that was replaced. That version admitted episodes that never reached today's 23 days below the EMA (N=15, NDX 12m median +24.9%, F3 +34.2%).

Whipsaw and re-entry counts depend on the Friday rebalance marks (holiday Fridays are skipped). The Nasdaq-100 is a survivor index with an exceptional history, so its base rates may overstate positive outcomes. These are conditional base rates, not forecasts.
